title: Managing Workflow Permissions
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of managing workflow permissions and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to managing workflow permissions.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on managing workflow permissions. The `permissions` key limits token scopes such as `contents`, `pull-requests`, `packages`, and `id-token`; least privilege is the default design objective. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Managing Workflow Permissions matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. The `permissions` key limits token scopes such as `contents`, `pull-requests`, `packages`, and `id-token`; least privilege is the default design objective. Security starts with least privilege and trust boundaries: scope tokens, store credentials as secrets, isolate untrusted contributions, and prefer short-lived federated credentials when available.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: The `permissions` key limits token scopes such as `contents`, `pull-requests`, `packages`, and `id-token`; least privilege is the default design objective. Security starts with least privilege and trust boundaries: scope tokens, store credentials as secrets, isolate untrusted contributions, and prefer short-lived federated credentials when available. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: The permissions keyword
items.text: Declare only the token scopes the job requires. A read-only job should not receive write access; verify permissions at workflow and job scope and review organization policy.

items.title: The principle of least privilege
items.text: For the principle of least privilege, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

content_blocks.code:
name: Grant only the permission this check needs
on: pull_request
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: read
jobs:
  inspect:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Read-only pull request validation"
content_blocks.expected_output: The workflow declares read-only repository and pull-request scopes; grant additional permissions only to the specific job that needs them.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain managing workflow permissions, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Constrain credentials and token permissions, and prefer scoped, short-lived authentication where supported.

troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
